benchmarks.summary: Serialize and deserialize one chat request of 50 messages. No network.
benchmarks.what: The cost of turning an OwnedChatRequest into JSON bytes and parsing those bytes back into an OwnedChatRequest.
benchmarks.why: Every model call pays this cost on the way out and on the way back. If this grows, the client is spending time on the envelope before any token arrives.
benchmarks.timing: fifty_messages() runs before the bench and builds the request once. The timed closure is b.iter, not iter_batched. Inside it: serde_json::to_vec of that request, serde_json::from_slice back to OwnedChatRequest, and black_box of the parsed value. Building the 50 messages is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 messages, alternating user and assistant, text question N and answer N. The model string is gpt-4o-mini. One request, reused for every sample.
benchmarks.fake: Nothing is mocked. This is serde_json on an in-memory struct. There is no provider, no socket, and no clock sleep.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This should stay well under a millisecond. A jump means the request type or the JSON layer got heavier, not that the model got slower.

benchmarks.summary: One mock completion that returns events, with zero simulated latency.
benchmarks.what: How long complete_events takes on MockProvider when the fake reply is the string ok and the configured latency is zero.
benchmarks.why: This is the floor under a turn that does not wait on a model. A regression here is harness overhead, not provider time.
benchmarks.timing: The multi-thread runtime (4 workers, time enabled) is built outside. MockProvider::with_latency("ok", Duration::ZERO) and the one user message hello are built outside. The timed closure is b.to_async(&rt).iter. Inside the async iter: complete_events on that message slice, then black_box of the events. Provider construction is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: One user message, content hello. The provider reply is the string ok.
benchmarks.fake: MockProvider is an in-memory fake. complete sleeps only when latency is non-zero; this bench sets Duration::ZERO, so the sleep is skipped. No HTTP client is built.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Hundreds of nanoseconds is the expected range. Milliseconds would mean the mock started waiting or allocating per call.

benchmarks.summary: One hundred concurrent mock completions on a four-worker runtime.
benchmarks.what: The time to spawn 100 MockProvider::complete calls, wait until every join handle finishes, and discard the replies.
benchmarks.why: A fan-out of tool-less calls should be scheduling and cloning, not 100 times one call stacked end to end. This shows whether the runtime overlaps the zero-latency mock.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (4 workers) and an Arc of MockProvider::with_latency("ok", Duration::ZERO) are built outside. The timed closure is b.to_async(&rt).iter. Inside the async block: clone the message vec, spawn 100 JoinSet tasks, and poll join_next until the set is empty. Each task clones the Arc and the messages again and calls complete. That cloning and the joins are inside the sample. Runtime startup is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 100 tasks. Each sees one user message hello. Reply text is ok. Concurrency is whatever 4 worker threads can run; the mock does not sleep.
benchmarks.fake: Same zero-latency MockProvider. complete records the messages it saw in a Mutex and returns an assistant message. No network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. It should be far below 100 times mock_turn_overhead, because the calls overlap and do not sleep. A number near 100 ms would mean the tasks are waiting on each other.

benchmarks.summary: Build a chat request, serialize it, and parse a canned response that is not that request.
benchmarks.what: The client-side work of assembling a ChatRequest, encoding it, and turning a fixed response body into events.
benchmarks.why: This is the OpenRouter-shaped envelope without the HTTP call. It catches a slower request builder or a heavier events_for_reply.
benchmarks.timing: The 50 user messages and the canned response bytes are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: construct ChatRequest with model openai/gpt-4o-mini, serde_json::to_vec of that request, serde_json::from_slice of the canned response (not of the bytes just written), events_for_reply on the first choice, and black_box of the pair. No connection is opened.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 user messages, question 0 through question 49. The canned body is a stop finish, model openai/gpt-4o-mini, assistant content ok, usage 50 prompt tokens, 1 completion token, 51 total, cost 0.25.
benchmarks.fake: The response is a byte string in the bench. It is not an HTTP response. Nothing is deserialized from the request that was just serialized.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A few microseconds is the right scale. This number does not include DNS, TLS, or token generation.

benchmarks.summary: Parse one reply that has usage and cost, and one reply that has a model and no usage.
benchmarks.what: events_for_reply on both shapes of a buffered ChatResponse, twice per sample.
benchmarks.why: A missing usage object and a different provider model are the edges the client has to accept. The bench is there so that path stays cheap.
benchmarks.timing: Both canned bodies are byte strings outside the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: from_slice of the usage body, from_slice of the no-usage body, events_for_reply for each, and black_box of the pair. No request is built and no socket is used.
benchmarks.inputs: First body: model openai/gpt-4o-mini, assistant content ok, usage with cost 0.25. Second body: model anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet, assistant content ok, no usage field.
benchmarks.fake: Both bodies are literals in the bench file. No HTTP, no mock server.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This is two small JSON parses plus event construction. It should stay under a millisecond.

benchmarks.summary: Submit one line to a fresh session inbox.
benchmarks.what: SessionInbox::submit of the string hello on an inbox whose capacity is 1.
benchmarks.why: The chat loop submits the user's line before it calls the model. This is that handoff on its own.
benchmarks.timing: iter_batched with BatchSize::SmallInput. The setup closure, which is not timed, builds SessionInbox::new(1). The timed closure calls inbox.submit("hello") and expects Ok. Criterion drops the inbox after the timed closure. There is no pop and no model call inside the sample.
benchmarks.inputs: One string, hello. Capacity 1, so a second submit would fail, but the bench submits once per sample on a new inbox.
benchmarks.fake: The inbox is an in-memory channel. No provider is constructed.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Tens of nanoseconds is a channel send. Microseconds would mean the submit path started allocating more than the line.

benchmarks.summary: One chat line through a session whose provider returns immediately.
benchmarks.what: ChatSession::handle_line("hello") when the line is not a slash command and the provider is a zero-latency mock.
benchmarks.why: This is the per-turn bookkeeping around the model: trim, inbox submit and pop, push the user message, trim_to, to_messages, complete_events, and push the assistant. It is the number to compare against a real provider call.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (4 workers, time enabled) is built outside. iter_batched with BatchSize::SmallInput on an async bench. The setup closure, not timed, builds ChatSession::new(MockProvider::new("ok"), "Be brief.", 8000). The timed async closure calls handle_line("hello") and black_box of the outcome. Session construction is excluded. handle_line trims, sees that hello is not a command, and calls ask.
benchmarks.inputs: System prompt Be brief. Token budget 8000. One user line hello. The mock reply is ok. The session is new for every sample, so history length is one user message plus the reply.
benchmarks.fake: MockProvider::new uses Duration::ZERO, so complete_events does not sleep. No file is saved or loaded. No network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Hundreds of nanoseconds means the turn overhead is still noise next to a model call. A millisecond here, with a zero-latency mock, is a regression in the session path.

benchmarks.summary: HashMap lookup of one tool in a registry of 50.
benchmarks.what: ToolRegistry::get("tool-25") and then Tool::kind on the result.
benchmarks.why: The dispatcher looks up every tool call by name. The lookup itself should be lost in the noise next to the tool body.
benchmarks.timing: registry_of(50) runs before the bench and registers tool-00 through tool-49. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: get("tool-25") and black_box of kind(). Registration is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 StaticTool values, each ToolKind::Read, names tool-00 to tool-49. The probed name is tool-25, which is present.
benchmarks.fake: StaticTool is an in-memory tool with no body call in this bench. No model and no MCP session.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A few tens of nanoseconds is a map hit. If this reaches microseconds, the registry stopped being a plain lookup.

benchmarks.summary: List the schemas of 50 tools in one gated toolset.
benchmarks.what: Catalog::available_schemas for an env where HARNESS_BENCH=1, then the length of that list.
benchmarks.why: The prompt is built from the tools the current env actually enables. This is that filter and schema list at a small catalog size.
benchmarks.timing: catalog_of(50) runs before the bench: one toolset named bench, gated on env HARNESS_BENCH, holding 50 StaticTools, plus an EnvMap with HARNESS_BENCH=1. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: available_schemas and black_box of the length. Building the catalog is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 read tools, names tool-00 to tool-49, one toolset. The gate is open because the env value is 1.
benchmarks.fake: StaticTool schemas are in memory. No process is spawned and no model is called.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Tens of microseconds for 50 schemas is the scale of this list. A large jump means schema cloning, not tool execution.

benchmarks.summary: Eight read tools that each sleep 1 ms, dispatched together with a bound of 8.
benchmarks.what: Dispatcher::new(8).run on eight LatencyTool reads. The sleeps overlap, so the batch should cost about one millisecond plus scheduling, not eight.
benchmarks.why: This is the reason the dispatcher exists. Sequential dispatch of the same eight tools is the comparison on the next row.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (8 workers, time enabled) is built outside. iter_batched with BatchSize::SmallInput on an async bench. The setup closure, not timed, calls batch(Duration::from_millis(1)), which registers read-0 through read-7 and builds eight empty-object ToolCalls. The timed async closure constructs Dispatcher::new(8), calls run, and black_box of the outputs. The 1 ms sleep is inside LatencyTool::call, so it is inside the sample. Tool registration is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Eight read-only tools, delay 1 ms each, arguments {}. Concurrency bound 8, so all eight may run at once. Worker threads: 8.
benchmarks.fake: LatencyTool sleeps with tokio::time::sleep and then returns its name. There is no model and no MCP server. A zero delay would not sleep; this delay is 1 ms.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better, but the floor is the 1 ms sleep. A result near 1–3 ms means the eight sleeps overlapped. A result near 8 ms means they ran one after another.

benchmarks.summary: The same eight 1 ms reads, run one after another.
benchmarks.what: Dispatcher::run_sequential on the same LatencyTool batch the concurrent bench uses.
benchmarks.why: The gap between this row and the concurrent row is the overlap the bound is supposed to buy. If they match, the concurrent path is not overlapping.
benchmarks.timing: Same setup as the concurrent bench. The runtime is outside. iter_batched setup builds the registry and the eight calls and is not timed. The timed async closure calls Dispatcher::new(8).run_sequential. The eight 1 ms sleeps happen inside that call, in order. Registration is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Eight LatencyTool reads named read-0 through read-7, each Duration::from_millis(1), empty JSON arguments.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory tools. The only wait is tokio::time::sleep inside the tool. No model.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better only within the sequential path. Expect about 8 ms, eight sleeps stacked. Much less than that means the sequential path started overlapping. Much more means overhead beyond the sleeps.

benchmarks.summary: One echo tool call over stdio to the local MCP fixture.
benchmarks.what: McpSession::call_text("echo", {"text": "ping"}) on a session that is already connected to the fixture child process.
benchmarks.why: This is the cost of one MCP round trip on stdio after the process is up: the request framing, the child, and the response. It is the baseline for the HTTP row.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (4 workers, all features) is built outside. McpSession::stdio(fixture_binary()) is connected with block_on before the bench. The timed closure is b.to_async(&runtime).iter. Inside: one call_text and black_box of the text. session.shutdown() runs after the bench function returns, so it is not part of the samples. Process spawn and the MCP handshake are excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: Tool name echo, argument text ping. One in-flight call. The fixture binary is the chapter 4 child.
benchmarks.fake: The fixture is a real local process, not OpenRouter. FIXTURE_DELAY_MS is not set, and the fixture sleeps only when that variable parses as a positive number, so echo returns the text without sleeping. No remote network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Tens to a couple of hundred microseconds is a local stdio round trip. Milliseconds mean the child started waiting or the session stopped reusing the pipe.

benchmarks.summary: One echo tool call over streamable HTTP to the fixture on loopback.
benchmarks.what: call_text echo ping on a session connected to HttpFixture's URL.
benchmarks.why: The same tool as the stdio bench, with HTTP framing on 127.0.0.1 instead of a pipe. The difference between the two rows is the transport.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime is built outside. HttpFixture::spawn(fixture_binary()) and McpSession::streamable_http(&fixture.url) both finish before the bench. The timed closure is one async call_text. Shutdown after the bench is not timed. Spawn and the HTTP handshake are excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: One echo call, text ping, against the fixture URL on loopback. FIXTURE_DELAY_MS is unset.
benchmarks.fake: A real child process listening on loopback. Not OpenRouter, and not a mocked TCP stack. The echo tool does not sleep.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Expect more than the stdio row and still well under a millisecond on loopback. A multi-millisecond result means a new connection per call or an accidental delay.

benchmarks.summary: Fifty echo calls through the dispatcher, bound 8, over one stdio session.
benchmarks.what: Dispatcher::new(DISPATCH_BOUND).run of 50 echo ToolCalls. DISPATCH_BOUND is 8, so at most eight calls are in flight.
benchmarks.why: This is the chapter 3 bound applied to a real MCP child. It should beat the sequential row by overlapping the process round trips.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (8 workers) is outside. Before the bench: spawn McpSession::stdio, register_remote into a ToolRegistry, and build 50 ToolCalls. Those steps are not timed. The timed async iter calls run and black_box of the output length. The session stays up across samples. FIXTURE_DELAY_MS is unset, so each echo does not sleep.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 calls, all named echo, arguments {"text": "ping"}. One shared stdio session. Bound 8.
benchmarks.fake: The fixture process is real. The tool does no simulated sleep. There is no model in this bench; the calls are built by the bench, not by a provider.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. It should be lower than mcp_50_sequential. If the two rows match, the bound is not overlapping calls on the one session.

benchmarks.summary: The same fifty echo calls, one at a time, over stdio.
benchmarks.what: Dispatcher::run_sequential of the 50 echo calls on a registered MCP session.
benchmarks.why: The comparison for the concurrent row. Sequential is the cost of 50 round trips stacked.
benchmarks.timing: Same excluded setup as the concurrent bench: runtime, stdio session, register_remote, and the 50 calls are ready before the timer. The timed async iter calls run_sequential and black_box of the length. No fixture delay.
benchmarks.inputs: 50 echo pings. Bound value is still passed to Dispatcher::new, but run_sequential does not overlap them.
benchmarks.fake: Real local fixture process, zero FIXTURE_DELAY_MS, no model.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better on this path, and it should stay above the concurrent row. A sequential result close to the concurrent result means the session was already serial.

benchmarks.summary: Construct a tool-list cache and list once. The Rust function is cache_cold.
benchmarks.what: The first tools/list through ToolListCache, including constructing the cache, against an already connected stdio session.
benchmarks.why: A cold list is what a new session pays before any tool call. The hit row is the same list when the cache is warm.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime and the stdio McpSession are built before the bench. The timed closure is b.to_async(&runtime).iter. Inside the async iter: ToolListCache::new(session clone) and cache.list(). Cache construction is inside the sample. The MCP handshake is outside. The criterion name is mcp_list_cold; the Rust function that registers it is cache_cold.
benchmarks.inputs: One fixture process. The list is whatever tools the fixture registers (echo, note, and the other fixture tools). No FIXTURE_DELAY_MS.
benchmarks.fake: Real stdio child. The list call is a real MCP request. No OpenRouter.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This includes a process round trip, so it should look like the stdio echo row, not like the cache hit. A hit-sized number means the list never left the process.

benchmarks.summary: A warm ToolListCache::list. The Rust function is cache_hit. The runtime is polled inside the sample.
benchmarks.what: cache.list() after one list has already filled the cache.
benchmarks.why: Repeated tools/list on a live session should be a memory hit. This is the number that must stay far below the cold list.
benchmarks.timing: Session connect, ToolListCache::new, and one block_on(cache.list()) warming call all happen before the bench. The timed closure is a synchronous b.iter. Inside that iter the bench calls runtime.block_on around cache.list(). The block_on poll is part of the sample. The criterion name is mcp_list_hit; the Rust function is cache_hit.
benchmarks.inputs: The warmed cache from the fixture's tool list. One session, reused.
benchmarks.fake: The warm list is real MCP data already stored on the cache. The hit should not send another tools/list. The fixture process is still the one connected before the bench.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A few hundred nanoseconds is a hit plus the block_on. If this climbs toward the cold-list time, the cache missed and talked to the child again.

benchmarks.summary: JSON-schema token estimate for a synthetic catalog of 1,000 tools.
benchmarks.what: schema_cost on 1,000 generated ToolCards, then black_box of the token count.
benchmarks.why: Putting every schema in the prompt is the cost this chapter is trying to avoid. 1,000 tools is the smaller of the two sizes.
benchmarks.timing: generate(1000) runs before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: schema_cost, which serializes every card's schema JSON and estimates tokens as characters divided by 4, rounded up. Generating the cards is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 1,000 deterministic ToolCards from generate. Names, descriptions, and one string field each. No live catalog.
benchmarks.fake: The catalog is synthetic. schema_cost is not a tokenizer and does not call a model. No MCP connection.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This is CPU for a JSON dump and a character count. A higher token count is a bigger prompt, which is worse even when the bench time is flat. The time itself should stay well under the 10,000-tool row.

benchmarks.summary: The same schema token estimate for 10,000 tools.
benchmarks.what: schema_cost on the 10,000-card catalog.
benchmarks.why: 10,000 tools is the size the chapter treats as too big to paste into the prompt. This row is that paste.
benchmarks.timing: generate(10000) is outside the timer. b.iter calls schema_cost and black_box of tokens. Card generation is excluded. The JSON serialization of all 10,000 schemas is inside.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 ToolCards from generate. Same shape as the 1,000-card catalog.
benchmarks.fake: Synthetic cards. No tokenizer, no network, no MCP.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Expect on the order of ten times the 1,000-tool row. Tens of milliseconds is the measured range. If this drops without the catalog shrinking, the estimate stopped walking the schemas.

benchmarks.summary: Build a BM25 index over 10,000 tool cards.
benchmarks.what: Bm25Index::build on one owned copy of the 10,000-card catalog.
benchmarks.why: Search is cheap only after the index exists. Rebuilds at a checkpoint pay this number.
benchmarks.timing: generate(10000) is outside. iter_batched with BatchSize::LargeInput. The setup closure clones the card vec and is not timed. The timed closure calls Bm25Index::build on that owned vec and black_box of the index. The clone is excluded; the build is included.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 synthetic ToolCards. One index build per sample.
benchmarks.fake: No embeddings and no MCP. The cards are the deterministic generate() catalog.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This is a batch cost, not a per-turn cost. It should be milliseconds to a few tens of milliseconds, not a per-keystroke number.

benchmarks.summary: BM25 search for the top 8 hits of "rename a file" over 10,000 tools.
benchmarks.what: Bm25Index::search on an index that was built once.
benchmarks.why: This is the per-turn search the model does not see directly: the harness picks a handful of tools instead of shipping 10,000 schemas.
benchmarks.timing: The index is built once before the bench, from the same 10,000 cards. That build is excluded. The timed closure is b.iter. Inside: search("rename a file", 8) and black_box of the hits.
benchmarks.inputs: Query rename a file. Limit 8. Index of 10,000 generated cards.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory BM25 over synthetic cards. No embedding model and no network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A search should be a small fraction of the index build. Hundreds of microseconds is the measured scale. Milliseconds per search would erase the win over pasting every schema.

benchmarks.summary: Token estimate for all 10,000 schemas, from the search-tool crate.
benchmarks.what: schema_cost on 10,000 cards, the full-prompt side of the comparison with the lazy prompt.
benchmarks.why: The next row is the prompt the model actually sees after search. This row is the cost of not searching.
benchmarks.timing: generate(10000) is outside. b.iter calls schema_cost and black_box of tokens. Generation is excluded. This is a separate bench from section 5.1's schema_tokens_10000; it lives in the search-tool crate.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 generated ToolCards.
benchmarks.fake: Synthetic catalog. Character-divided-by-4 token estimate. No model.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better, and it should stay far above lazy_visible_prompt_10000. If the two rows meet, the lazy prompt started including the whole catalog.

benchmarks.summary: Render the prompt after one search has already selected tools.
benchmarks.what: ToolSession::visible_prompt after search_tools and begin_turn have already run.
benchmarks.why: This is the bytes the model would see once the catalog is narrowed. It should be a tiny fraction of shipping every schema.
benchmarks.timing: Before the bench: ToolSession::new(generate(10000), 8), search_tools("rename a file", 8), and begin_turn(). All of that is excluded. The timed closure is b.iter around visible_prompt() only.
benchmarks.inputs: A session over 10,000 cards, search limit 8, query rename a file, one turn already begun.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory ToolSession and the synthetic catalog. No model call.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Microseconds means the visible prompt is a slice of an already chosen set. If it climbs toward the full-schema row, the prompt is walking the whole catalog again.

benchmarks.summary: Routed search for 8 tools in a 10,000-card catalog.
benchmarks.what: Router::search("rename a file", 8) on a router built once.
benchmarks.why: Routing is the chapter's way of keeping search inside the servers that can answer. This is that search after the router exists.
benchmarks.timing: generate(10000) and Router::build run before the bench and are excluded. b.iter calls router.search and black_box of the hits.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 cards, query rename a file, limit 8.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory router over synthetic cards. No network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. It should stay in the same band as the BM25 search, not in the index-build band.

benchmarks.summary: Prepare every card against the full name set, then serialize the schemas.
benchmarks.what: prepare_card for all 10,000 cards, then schema_json of the prepared list.
benchmarks.why: Shrinking is only a win if the prepare-and-serialize step is cheaper than the prompt it replaces. This row is that step at the full catalog, which is the worst case.
benchmarks.timing: The card vec and a HashSet of every card name are built outside. b.iter maps prepare_card over every card, calls schema_json, and black_box of the string. The name set is excluded. Walking all 10,000 cards is inside.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 cards. The name set contains every tool name, so prepare sees the full catalog as known names.
benchmarks.fake: Synthetic cards. No model.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. This is a full-catalog walk, so it is allowed to be slower than a search. It should not sneak into the per-turn path.

benchmarks.summary: First list() on a cache of 10,000 synthetic tools.
benchmarks.what: ListCache::list when the cache is dirty, which clones the generated cards out of SyntheticSource.
benchmarks.why: The cold list stands in for the first tools/list. The hit row is the same call once the Arc is filled.
benchmarks.timing: iter_batched with BatchSize::LargeInput. The setup closure, not timed, calls ListCache::new(10_000), which builds the synthetic source and leaves the cache dirty. The timed closure calls cache.list() and black_box of the Arc. new() is excluded. The first list, including the clone into the cache, is included.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 generated cards behind SyntheticSource. No chapter 4 client is attached. list_calls starts at 0.
benchmarks.fake: SyntheticSource::list is an in-memory stand-in for MCP tools/list. It clones the vec and increments list_calls. No process and no network.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. A cold list of 10,000 cards is milliseconds. It should stay far above the hit. If cold and hit match, the cache was already warm inside the timed closure.

benchmarks.summary: list() after the 10,000-card cache has been filled.
benchmarks.what: A second ListCache::list, which clones the cached Arc and does not call the source again.
benchmarks.why: Turns after the first should not rebuild the catalog. This is that hit.
benchmarks.timing: ListCache::new(10_000) and one list() run before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter around cache.list(). The warming list is excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: One warm cache of 10,000 cards.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory SyntheticSource. The hit must not increment the source's list count.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Nanoseconds means an Arc clone. Anything in the millisecond range means the cache missed and generated the catalog again.

benchmarks.summary: Filter 10,000 cards down to the servers one agent is allowed to see.
benchmarks.what: AgentView::filter for an agent named files-agent whose only server is files.
benchmarks.why: A per-agent view is how the catalog stays large while one prompt stays small. The filter has to be cheap next to search.
benchmarks.timing: The warm cache's list() result and AgentView::new("files-agent", ["files"]) are built outside. b.iter calls view.filter on that card slice and black_box of the result. Listing and view construction are excluded.
benchmarks.inputs: 10,000 cards from the warm cache. One agent, one allowed server name: files.
benchmarks.fake: In-memory cards and an in-memory view. No model and no MCP session.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Tens of microseconds is a scan of 10,000 cards. If this approaches the cold-list time, the filter started copying schemas it should not.

benchmarks.summary: check_gate on a fresh flag, a default budget, and zero usage.
benchmarks.what: How long the pre-call gate takes when nothing is cancelled and nothing has been spent.
benchmarks.why: The loop calls this before every model call. It has to stay noise next to even a mock completion.
benchmarks.timing: CancelFlag::new, Budget::default, AgentUsage::default, and Instant::now are created before the bench. The timed closure is b.iter around check_gate of those four values. Construction is excluded. The flag is not cancelled and the default budget is not exceeded, so the function returns None. The loop itself is not called. This row is the 6.1 live tool body crate. The workflow deletes target/criterion after the section so a later section cannot overwrite it. Older artifacts stored one mean per function name, and those means are seeded on section 6.10 because that section ran last.
benchmarks.inputs: One unused cancel flag, the default budget, default usage, and a start instant from before the samples.
benchmarks.fake: No provider, no tools, and no sleep. The flag and the budget are real types with nothing tripped.
benchmarks.reading: Smaller is better. Single-digit to low tens of nanoseconds is the range. A microsecond means the gate started doing more than a couple of comparisons.

benchmarks.summary: One scripted final answer through this section's run_loop. No tool call.
benchmarks.what: The time for a turn whose model reply is the text ok and whose registry is empty.
benchmarks.why: This is the loop overhead with the model replaced by a script. Section 6.1 is the loop before the later checks. Section 6.10 is the same bench shape on the finished loop. Comparing them is the cost of those checks.
benchmarks.timing: The runtime (4 workers), an empty ToolRegistry, and Dispatcher::new(DISPATCH_BOUND) are built outside. DISPATCH_BOUND is 8. The timed closure is b.to_async(&runtime).iter. Inside the async iter: a new ScriptedProvider that returns one text reply ok, a user message status, and await run_loop. Section 6.1's run_loop calls check_gate, then provider.complete on the messages, and returns Finished when the reply has no tool calls.
